newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FORECAST - SWEDISH LONG BOND YIELDS SEEN RISING.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - SWEDISH LONG BOND YIELDS SEEN RISING.

text.p: Long Swedish bond yields are expected to rise both in the short and long term but the spread to Germany is seen narrowing and the crown seen firming, a monthly Reuter poll of 14 economists showed on Monday.

While yields are expected to be pushed higher by international trends, the spread is expected to narrow as the risk premium investors put on Sweden will decrease, said Knut Hallberg, economist at Swedbank.
"We expect a lower Swedish risk premium as convergence trading is expected to continue and Sweden will be part of it," Hallberg said.
"In addition, Swedish fundamentals look OK."
Swedbank does not expect Sweden to be among the first wave of countries to join Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
"If (Sweden) would say yes (to EMU participation) the figures would look completely different," Hallberg said, adding that interest rates in that case would be lower.
Economists polled expected the spread to Germany to fall to 102 basis points in one year, from 120 at Friday's close.

They saw the ten-year bond yield rising to 7.50 percent in a year, but expected it to fall to 7.10 percent in a month from Friday's close of 7.21 percent. In three months, economists saw the yield trading at 7.14 percent.
Eleven of the 14 economists believed in further repo rate cuts in the second quarter, expecting the repo to bottom out at 3.80 percent. It currently stands at 4.10 percent.

In one month, the repo was seen at 4.05 percent and in three months at 3.90 percent. In one year, economists expected a repo of 4.0 percent on average, with forecasts ranging from 3.50 percent to 4.35 percent.
The central bank, the Riksbank, cut the repo rate 25 times last year, bringing it down to its current level of 4.10 percent from 8.91 percent.
The repo is the bank's key tool for controlling money market activity.
Economists said the weak, volatile crown had kept the Riksbank from moving its key rate so far this year.

"I think year-on-year inflation will keep being zero or minus this year and in that case I don't see any reason for not cutting once more, or a couple of times," said Erik Jonsen, trader at Atlas Copco.
"Deflation is a larger threat than inflation."
Jonsen expected the repo to bottom at 3.75 percent in June.
"The Riksbank's reason not to cut the rate has been the soft crown," Jonsen said. "But the crown weakening is not just a real crown weakening, it partly stems from a strong dollar."
The six-month T-bill is expected to fall in the shortterm, only to rise as economic trends pick up.
"I believe that we so far have weak economic trends and that the Riksbank would like to cut the repo rate," said Carl Nilsson, trader at Swedish Match.
He forecast the six-month T-bill rate would fall to 4.00 percent in a month and rise to 4.60 percent in a year from Friday's close of 4.13 percent.
Economists expected the crown to firm to 4.3950 against the mark in three months and to be trading at 4.4350 in a year, compared to its late Friday level of 4.4570.

Economists interviewed for the poll were from AGA, ABB, Aragon, Atlas Copco, Carnegie, Den Danske Bank, Hagstromer & Qviberg, NCC, Nordbanken, Postgirot Bank, S-E-Banken, Skandia, Swedish Match, and Swedbank.
Den Danske Bank did not give forecasts for the ten-year bond yield and for six-month T-bills, while Hagstromer & Qviberg did not give forecasts for six-month T-bills.
-- Charlotte Meynert, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1071
